name: Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data
title: Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data
answer: Federated sharing of sensitive data covers arrangements in which several organisations analyse a combined dataset without any one of them handing over the raw records. It sits inside research data management and repository practice, where the unit of interest is often a cohort, a clinical trial, or a national statistics collection that cannot lawfully leave its home institution. The scope includes the technical protocol, the data-sharing agreement, the access committee, and the audit trail that together make a joint analysis possible. It is distinct from simply publishing a de-identified extract, because the data stay under local control throughout.

sections.body: Federated sharing of sensitive data covers arrangements in which several organisations analyse a combined dataset without any one of them handing over the raw records. It sits inside research data management and repository practice, where the unit of interest is often a cohort, a clinical trial, or a national statistics collection that cannot lawfully leave its home institution. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a federation of nodes, each holding its own data behind its own firewall, plus a coordination layer that distributes code rather than records. Common building blocks are containerised analysis environments, a secure query or model-training protocol, and a registry that records which datasets exist and who may query them. Repositories and trusted research environments supply the storage and the identity checks, while the coordinating body supplies the common schema and the software stack. Because only summary statistics or model updates travel between sites, the network requirements are modest compared with moving the underlying files.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical study begins with a common data model so that each site can map its local variables to shared definitions, followed by a protocol approved by every participating ethics or access committee. Analysts then send the same code to each node, run it locally, and return aggregate results or encrypted model parameters to a central aggregator. Iterative methods such as federated averaging repeat this loop until the combined model converges, and sites may add noise or threshold small counts before anything leaves. Documentation of the exact code version, the query log, and the aggregation rules is what makes the result reproducible.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on the fact that the data never move, so the legal basis rests on each site's own consent, licence, or statutory permission rather than on a single transfer agreement. Provenance must record which sites contributed, under which approval, and with which disclosure controls, because a reader of the output cannot inspect the inputs. Residual risks include inference from repeated queries, membership disclosure through model outputs, and re-identification when small cells are reported. Governance therefore combines a data-sharing agreement, a publication and output-checking policy, and an access committee that can suspend a query or a site.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward standardised federated protocols and reusable node software, so that a new study can join an existing network instead of rebuilding one. Expect closer integration with repository metadata, so that a federated dataset can be cited and versioned like any other research object, and more attention to output disclosure control as a formal step in the pipeline. Regulators and funders are likely to ask for evidence that federation was used where data could not be pooled, which pushes the field toward auditable, portable implementations. The open question is whether coordination costs fall enough for small repositories to participate alongside large consortia.
